content: The target population for tuberculosis (TB) interventions includes children and adolescents under 15 years of age who present for care at district hospitals or primary healthcare (PHC) facilities, either through outpatient visits or systematic TB screening. This also includes children under 15 years identified with presumptive TB through routine clinical assessments or systematic screening at these healthcare levels. Patient-level interventions implemented include systematic TB screening, clinical evaluations, testing using Xpert Ultra on nasopharyngeal aspirates (NPA), stool, or sputum samples, optimized chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation using digital radiography, improved reading skills, simplified tools, quality control, and treatment decision-making. Health system-level interventions included decentralization strategies. At the district hospital level, a patient-centered diagnostic approach for childhood TB was implemented, with PHC facilities conducting systematic TB screening and referring cases to district hospitals. Similarly, at the PHC level, systematic TB screening, clinical evaluations, and testing using Xpert Ultra on NPA, stool, or sputum samples were conducted. The TB-Speed project aimed to strengthen pediatric TB services for early detection. Feedback from healthcare implementers highlighted that systematic screening was valuable but challenging to implement, particularly at district hospitals due to high workloads and patient flow. Screening questions were sometimes difficult for parents to understand, especially in crowded waiting areas or in contexts where TB stigma exists. Stool collection and NPA using battery-operated mucus aspirators were feasible and well-accepted at both district hospitals and PHC levels. However, NPA collection often required two individuals (a healthcare worker and a colleague or the child’s parent). Stool samples were frequently not obtained during the child’s visit due to logistical and financial constraints for parents to return with stool containers. Xpert Ultra testing using the GeneXpert Edge platform was implemented in PHC facilities across six countries, with stool samples tested at district hospitals. However, poor sample transport conditions (e.g., long distances, difficult terrain, heavy rain, and storage temperature issues) and power instability at district hospitals and PHC levels affected stool sample testing. Additionally, digitization and transfer of CXR images for clinician access were challenging in several countries due to poor internet connectivity, particularly at PHC levels. Both decentralization models faced structural and organizational constraints, including frequent staff rotations, lack of motivation, and the need for incentives for additional workloads. Supportive supervision helped address operational challenges, and clinical mentoring increased clinicians’ confidence in diagnosing TB and interpreting CXRs. In Uganda, a project implemented between 2015 and 2016 focused on decentralizing TB healthcare services for children from tertiary to PHC facilities. It also established linkages to support community-based household contact screening and management. District-level trainers were trained in childhood TB management and subsequently trained frontline health workers at PHC levels through two-day didactic sessions enhanced with case studies. Community health workers (CHWs) were trained to screen household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases, refer symptomatic contacts for evaluation, and provide health education and adherence support for TB preventive treatment (TPT). Post-training mentorship and supportive supervision were conducted monthly for the first three months and then quarterly. Health system strengthening included repairing faulty microscopes, retraining laboratory personnel, and improving supply chain management. In Ethiopia, a high TB burden country, interventions between 2016 and 2017 included incorporating a TB case management flowchart into the national Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) chart booklet, adding a TB screening column to the IMNCI treatment register, and providing sensitization training on pediatric TB. On-site coaching was provided for specimen collection using nasogastric aspiration techniques. Monitoring was conducted monthly and quarterly, with periodic performance review meetings. Decentralized childhood TB services, including sample collection, were successfully implemented at PHC levels using IMNCI platforms. In India, the CaP-TB project (2018–2021) aimed to improve TB care quality in the private sector, including the prescription and uptake of standardized public fixed-dose combinations (FDCs). The project linked over 1,100 children and adolescents under 15 years with TB to public FDCs, increasing the proportion of children treated with government FDCs from 29% to 65%. Challenges included delays in treatment initiation due to medicine delivery logistics, inconvenient public pharmacy hours, and caregiver concerns about the pill burden for children in higher weight bands. Some private providers continued prescribing private-sector FDCs due to past favorable outcomes or doubts about the quality of public-sector FDCs. Differentiated service delivery (DSD), a people-centered approach initially applied to HIV care, can also be adapted for TB care. DSD simplifies and adapts services to meet the diverse needs of individuals, optimizing health system resources. For TB, this approach can enhance patient-centered care, particularly for children, adolescents, and those with HIV-associated TB. Integration of TB care into DSD models requires adaptations at national, facility, and community levels, including leadership enhancement, guideline adjustments, capacity-building, and alignment of logistics and reporting systems. Family-centered models for antiretroviral therapy (ART) that include children and caregivers can incorporate TPT, improving clinical outcomes and reducing travel and costs. However, fewer visits under DSD models may reduce opportunities for TB screening, necessitating careful alignment of TB and HIV services.
